awd_titl_txt: DDRIG: Digital Diagrams: Embodied Numeracy and Knowledge Visualization in the Middle Ages
awd_abstract_narration:
This project examines the importance of visualization and embodiment in understanding numbers. Specifically, it investigates a diagrammatic and gestural tradition central to medieval mathematics, culture, and daily life: the ancient tradition of finger-counting. For centuries, people depicted and performed numbers using the same powerful finger‑counting system which allowed counting to one million only using the hands. This in-depth study of the medieval finger-counting tradition contributes to the history of mathematics and computation. The project also engages broader audiences by creating an open-source database, developing an undergraduate course, and sharing findings at international conferences.  

The grant will support data collection and archival research. Over one hundred medieval manuscripts and early printed books will be examined and visual, textual, and material data will be collected. This work provide insights into premodern numeracy, embodied cognition, and knowledge transmission, contributing to science and technology studies, art history, and medieval studies. The project will illuminate how historical practices of visualization and embodiment shaped numerical cognition in the medieval period and will enhance our understanding of premodern numeracy and its implications for cognitive science and the history of technology.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project explores a technology important to ancient and medieval mathematics, culture, and daily life: the fingers. For centuries, people used a powerful finger-numeration system to represent numbers up to one million using only their hands. This method could support arithmetic, communication, trade, and teaching.

From classical authors such as Quintilian to medieval mathematicians such as Leonardo Fibonacci and Renaissance humanists such as Pierio Valeriano, many writers, readers, scribes, artists, monks, merchants, and teachers bore witness to the circulation, longevity, and power of this digital system.

By examining this tradition, the project explored how people in the past used the body, images, and books to understand and transmit numerical ideas.

During the award period, the project supported archival research in major manuscript and rare book collections in Europe and the United States. This research focused on medieval manuscripts and early printed books that preserve texts and images related to finger-reckoning and premodern numeracy. The materials consulted helped clarify how numerical knowledge circulated across different kinds of books, disciplines, and historical contexts.

The project’s findings contribute to the history of mathematics, computation, and science by showing that numerical thinking has not always depended primarily on written symbols or mechanical devices. In medieval contexts, gestures, diagrams, memory, and material books also played important roles in how numbers were taught, represented, and understood. This perspective helps broaden the history of computation by including embodied and visual practices alongside more familiar histories of notation and machines.

The award also supported several broader-impact outcomes. Research connected to the project was presented at major scholarly conferences. The project also contributed to ongoing dissertation research on embodied numeracy and visualization in the long Middle Ages.

A major public outcome was the creation of an open-access website (fingercounting.com). The site presents selected historical texts, translations, images, commentary, and an interactive simulator that allows users to explore historical finger-reckoning gestures. It is intended for scholars, students, educators, and general readers.

The project also supported the development of an undergraduate course on the history of analog computing. Together, these outcomes make a little-known chapter in the history of mathematics and computation accessible to both specialist and public audiences.
